questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The location, the nature and wildlife around, interesting subjects (that KU doesn't offer) and language (English)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I rate my experience 10/10 - everything wasn't perfect of course, I did have some challenges - that is life, but everything else was seriously beyond amazing. James Cook university is perfect for someone who loves nature and wants to be immersed in wild life, while also having really interesting subjects and a great social community at uni. It is perfect if you want to be around a bunch of people who loves being adventurous and nerdy about nature and wildlife.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy - a bit overwhelming because of the big amounts of information, but I had gotten a bunch of e-mails beforehand and key was just to ask at the student central. Most information will be given to you as long as you show up to the information events in the beginning.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Got a bunch of information at events and got picked up at the airport by uni-staff, shown around at my dorm, and Student central was ready to help with anything - also things that were not uni-related.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
6 Colleges were available.

2 of the colleges, Saint Catholics and John Flynn, were mostly for Australian students who were pretty young as well. Did not know any people living there - only a few who moved out. 

The 4 others were filled with both Australian and international students:
Town Houses: Apartments with kitchens and laundry facilities in each - 7-11 people living together I think. Very close to class rooms and school facilities and the bus stop. I got the impression that the social life was not very big here, but it would depend on the people living in your flat. People here are more independent, and it attracts some of the older students.

Burrulga Yumba: Big very new building, everyone has their own room and everyone shares one giant kitchen. Shared bathrooms and showers on each floor. Great new facilities, like music room, pool tables and common roof top area, but social life can be a bit harder here, because you aren't associated with a group - like a shared flat, a hall group or a floor group. It can give a bit of hotel vibes. It is also very close to classrooms and such. I think there are social events planned as well, which is great for meeting people.

Rotary international house: flats 6-7 people with private rooms, shared bathrooms and kitchen. On the edge of campus, so plenty of wildlife around. If you live with some nice people, it is super cozy - I had a lot of friends living there in one apartment together, and I basically lived on their porch, they had a great time living there, but I also heard of people struggling with their flatmates and not enjoying it very much, but that is always a risk living with other people. Social life is mostly dependent on your flat, but there are a few events arranged by unilodge as well. A lot of international students here - but also some Australians.

George Roberts Hall: flats for 3-4 people with private rooms, shared living room and tea kitchen and shared bathrooms, and then a big dining hall with 3 meals a day - so this option is catered, which also makes it more expensive. It is also on the edge of campus and has wildlife visiting. Mix of Australian and international students. I lived here even though I wanted to live somewhere else, but I ended up enjoying it a lot. I saved a lot of time not having to go grocery shopping and cooking (supermarket is not very close to campus), which was nice because you will have so many plans and things to do as an exchange student. With GR you also get a free gym membership and a free coffee everyday. GR is extremely social as well - I met so many people just by eating in the dining hall, and the people living there arranges many social events all the time.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Saints, John Flynn and GR are catered, the rest have shared kitchens as described above.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Living on campus is great because almost everything happens here or starts here and public transportation is not the best in Townsville. And biking can be challenging in the town as well, so if you live off campus, which many of my friends also really enjoyed, I recommend finding a place not too far from campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you apply via unilodge, apply as early as possible - EVEN if you don't have your visa yet! They ask for your visa, but you can just write that you will provide it, when it arrives, they don't mind!

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: First we had to enrol in the subjects and then later we had to register for classes in each subject – each subject has some options for workshops/tutorials so you can “design” your own timetable. This although also means you have to find every subject’s timetable on JCU’s website to make sure you can design a timetable without overlap between your subjects. The website was a bit difficult to navigate in that regard.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I got some emails with instructions, I looked at JCU’s website a lot, and you can always email or call student service. When I got to JCU there is also a desk with staff ready to help – and they are really good at that.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all subjects and classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: My advice would be to enrol and register right away. Some subjects – like coral reef ecology, which I had – are very popular and have a student limit, so I registered as soon as it opened. You can also change classes and subjects even after classes have started – so I would rather register fast and then change later if needed, than wait until I was Australia.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had three 3rd year courses, and we had these together with master students, only difference were the demands for their reports and the number of assignments. Level was although fitting – some subjects harder than others of course. I found the level of the assignments a bit higher than at KU, which I had to get used to, but I also think I learned a lot form it.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Lectures and workshops/tutorials were basically the same as at KU. We had a lot of hands-on work, there are some really cool field trips and they use a lot of guest teachers from companies, research groups and organizations, which is really cool. More assignments though, since the exam won’t count a 100% of your grade. Each assignment will be a percentage of the final grade, and therefore I think they have a bit higher expectations than what I have been used to at KU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology AQ3007
Marine Conservation Biology MB3200
Coral Reef Ecology MB3190
People of Australia: Multiculturalism and indigeneity SS1010

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend all the subjects I took but especially these:

Aquatic Animal Ecophysiology AQ3007: Really good teacher (Jan Strugnell), very well organised and lots of hands-on work in labs. I enjoyed it a lot. (Even though it is an aqua culture subject it does not revolve around aquaculture – it is just as useful for biologists for example).

Coral Reef Ecology MB3190: A subject you can’t get many other places, very interesting, probably the hardest subject I had as well. Morgan Pratchett was the teacher, and he was quite ruthless but also a big shot in the field – I think he is taking a break from teaching though. We had a really cool field trip to Orpheus Island where we did field work in the coral reefs around the island, which was an amazing opportunity.

People of Australia: Multiculturalism and indigeneity SS1010: This was a first-year social science subject and the work load was less than the other subjects, which was really nice, since you really have a filled schedule as an exchange student. It was really interesting to learn about the Australian society with focus on the people and especially Aboriginal people. I don’t think I would have experienced Australia in the same way without this subject – I learned a lot. Many of my friends wish they had taken this subject or something similar.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Had to pay 400 dollars for a health insurance that the university requires you to have, which I didn’t expect since I already had my own insurance. I did end up spending a lot of money on small trips and diving – a bit more than expected. Other than that, no real unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is bit cheaper than in Denmark and public transportation was cheap in Townsville.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Would have enjoyed a bit more options to play sports for fun - but otherwise there are many clubs and stuff to do!!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There were a bunch of clubs like finstitute, zoology society, JCU dive club, JCU Marine society, Red Frogs (Christian group), bible studies I think and much more.
There was also a gym with weekly classes, and you could make a team of friends and join social sport, where different friend groups play against each other every week in different sports. 
The colleges on campus also had sports teams and theatre, band, choir and dance – All these groups would practice a few times a week and then compete against the other colleges in the end.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I really enjoyed social sport because it is a fun way to hang out and you get to try some Australian sports like netball and touch footy.
JCU dive Club was amazing –  Really cool people and some of my best memories from Australia has been on the liveaboards with this club. Whe you are right by the Great Barrier Reef you have to go diving.

Zoology Society – this was such a nice club, super nerdy and fun people, and everyone can be a part of it, no matter how nerdy you are yourself. They often arrange night walks, which costs no money and is such an easy way to hang out and find some cool animals. Wish I went on some more trips with these guys.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the strand, Visit Magnetic Island (go snorkelling, diving, hiking, lay on the beach, stay overnight, so much to do here), “study” at Riverway lagoon, stroll around Ross River or take a dip, go to night markets and Sunday markets in town, visit Crystal creek and Alligator Creek, take a trip to Cairns, Daintree and Mission Beach, go diving!!!, go whale watching. After our exams I went on a road trip down the east coast with friends, which I of course can also really recommend.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to the people in your classes, on your college and in the different clubs. Not being afraid of talking to new people and taking initiative to hang out is key.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Their extreme air condition threw my body off. No real challenges though.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Love Australian slang and humor! I also enjoyed trying some Australian sports and I really appreciated how chill and kind people in Australia are.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
The application process is slow and draining – but it is worth it, it just needs to be done, and everything will work out. My tip is just to do everything right away and check all your email accounts frequently – don’t postpone these things.

Don’t worry too much about school and grades. Have fun and go on all the trips – you will be fine, trust me.

Try new things! Try a sport you haven’t tried before, go on a trip with new people, join a club about something you know nothing about, try a subject you didn’t expect, talk to people you haven’t talked to before.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Maybe get in contact with someone going the same place as you or someone who has been there. I found that helpful in the application process.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing Australia with adventurous people passionate about biology - the friendships and all the experiences we got together.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Greatest challenge was probably adjusting to the college I lived in, because I didn’t get to live at the colleges that I initially wanted to - but I ended up really enjoying where I lived anyways!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
No matter where you end up going on exchange, it will be worth it, I think. I have never heard of anyone regretting going on exchange. And regarding choosing between the different universities – obviously it plays a big role, but in the end it is almost always the friendships and the experiences that count the most.

And when you fill out this evaluation after your stay, write in a word document and then copy paste it in, because otherwise everything you have written might get deleted if you use too long…

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
